ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: The study protocol was approved by the Life and Medical Sciences Research Ethics Committee at UCL (approval number 59875/008).
Participants were not informed about the neurotype of their interaction partners.
After the online session, subjects completed final questionnaires (see section 1 in Supplement for details) and were debriefed and thanked for their participation.

Volunteers were recruited through participant databases of the Institute of Cognitive Neuroscience at the University College London (UK) and the Center for Brain and Cognition at the Universitat Pompeu Fabra (Barcelona, Spain).

Autistic participants were additionally recruited via X (Twitter), Prolific, UK-based autistic charity organizations (Autistica, Center for ADHD and Autism Support), internal communication within AIMS-2-TRIALS, informal peer networks within the autistic community, and the University of Sheffield's autistic contact list.
Non-autistic participants were additionally recruited via study flyers at University College London campuses.

All participants provided electronic informed consent forms and received financial compensation for their participation: €10 per hour for Spain-based participants or £10 per hour for UK-based participants.
Recruited volunteers were autistic or non-autistic adults between 20 and 35 years of age, fluent in English or Spanish, and with no self-reported learning disability nor speech impairment.
Autistic participants were required to confirm having a clinical autism diagnosis (e.g., Autism Spectrum Disorder, Asperger's Syndrome).

Non-autistic participants were excluded if they were under the care of a psychologist or psychiatrist (i.e., an NHS professional for UK-based participants or a clinical psychologist/psychiatrist for Spain-based participants).

^^^Note: Participants were asked whether they know anyone who is autistic; response options were: F = yes, a family member/partner, C = yes, a close person (e.g., a friend), NC = yes, not a close person (e.g., work colleague), N = no.
Participants were never informed of others' neurotypes, and they never explicitly revealed their status in the study.
Each participant completed four dyadic interactions: two same-neurotype and two mixed-neurotype, yielding a total of 12 interactions per session.
Participants were assigned in pairs to three simultaneous breakout rooms across four interaction rounds.

After each interaction, participants completed a brief questionnaire rating their current states (stress, tiredness, anxiety) and evaluating the most recent interaction with another participants in terms of rapport and social motivation (more ratings were assessed in the study which are beyond the scope of this paper).
Participants were then allocated a new partner for the subsequent round.
Following the videoconference session, participants completed a post-experimental questionnaire with autism-related items (see Table 1).

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

summary_table.ethics_statements: The study protocol was approved by the Life and Medical Sciences Research Ethics Committee at UCL (approval number 59875/008).
live_data_statements: Participants were not informed about the neurotype of their interaction partners.
After the online session, subjects completed final questionnaires (see section 1 in Supplement for details) and were debriefed and thanked for their participation.

Volunteers were recruited through participant databases of the Institute of Cognitive Neuroscience at the University College London (UK) and the Center for Brain and Cognition at the Universitat Pompeu Fabra (Barcelona, Spain).

Autistic participants were additionally recruited via X (Twitter), Prolific, UK-based autistic charity organizations (Autistica, Center for ADHD and Autism Support), internal communication within AIMS-2-TRIALS, informal peer networks within the autistic community, and the University of Sheffield's autistic contact list.
Non-autistic participants were additionally recruited via study flyers at University College London campuses.

All participants provided electronic informed consent forms and received financial compensation for their participation: €10 per hour for Spain-based participants or £10 per hour for UK-based participants.
Recruited volunteers were autistic or non-autistic adults between 20 and 35 years of age, fluent in English or Spanish, and with no self-reported learning disability nor speech impairment.
Autistic participants were required to confirm having a clinical autism diagnosis (e.g., Autism Spectrum Disorder, Asperger's Syndrome).

Non-autistic participants were excluded if they were under the care of a psychologist or psychiatrist (i.e., an NHS professional for UK-based participants or a clinical psychologist/psychiatrist for Spain-based participants).

^^^Note: Participants were asked whether they know anyone who is autistic; response options were: F = yes, a family member/partner, C = yes, a close person (e.g., a friend), NC = yes, not a close person (e.g., work colleague), N = no.
Participants were never informed of others' neurotypes, and they never explicitly revealed their status in the study.
Each participant completed four dyadic interactions: two same-neurotype and two mixed-neurotype, yielding a total of 12 interactions per session.
Participants were assigned in pairs to three simultaneous breakout rooms across four interaction rounds.

After each interaction, participants completed a brief questionnaire rating their current states (stress, tiredness, anxiety) and evaluating the most recent interaction with another participants in terms of rapport and social motivation (more ratings were assessed in the study which are beyond the scope of this paper).
Participants were then allocated a new partner for the subsequent round.
Following the videoconference session, participants completed a post-experimental questionnaire with autism-related items (see Table 1).
To avoid data leakage, folds were assigned at the participant level so that all observations from a given subject were kept within the same fold.

To preserve the clustered structure of the data, duplicated bootstrap copies of the same participant were assigned unique bootstrap-specific IDs, and 10-fold cross-validation within each bootstrap sample was defined at this new ID level.
Panel A) Each participant took part in one of 10 online sessions (5 in English and 5 in Spanish), in which they interacted with two persons of their neurotype and two of the other neurotype.

text.text: Social connection is often conceptualized as an individual competence, yet it fundamentally unfolds through dynamic coordination between people.
To test what drives social connection across diverse interaction styles, we examined naturalistic conversations between autistic and non-autistic adults using a round-robin design.

We combined multimodal behavioral tracking-spanning dozens of behaviors across facial expression, head movement, vocal prosody, and turn-taking-with dispositional profiling across same-and mixed-neurotype dyads.
Non-autistic dyads reported higher rapport than mixed pairs.
While individual dispositions (traits, states) shaped evaluations, non-verbal synchrony emerged as the sole behavioral predictor of rapport across all dyad types.
In contrast, none of the individual behaviors were linked to connection.
Autistic participants showed greater motivation to interact again with their partners.

By demonstrating that rapport operates through interpersonal coordination even across contrasting communicative profiles of autistic and non-autistic adults, these findings establish that social connection is an emergent property of interacting minds.

text.text: Social interaction is a dynamic, multidirectional process.
An individual's disposition, behaviors, and perspectives interact with those of their interlocutor, and with situational context (Monnier et al., 2025).

text.text: Individual cognitive and motivational traits and reciprocal interaction together create 'social feedback loops' (West et al., 2026) allowing rapport and other social qualities to emerge between people.

text.text: While neuroscience and psychology have traditionally focused on social cognition from the perspective of an individual observer, there has been a surge of studies investigating real-time, person-to-person interactions (Jaegher et al., 2010; Schilbach et al., 2013).

text.text: These aim to answer the longstanding question of how people connect with each other, and why this process is not equally easy for everyone.

As difficulties in social interaction are a core characteristic of Autism Spectrum Disorder (hereafter: autism) (American Psychiatric Association, 2013), autism provides a valuable lens for understanding the complexity and variability of human interaction.

text.text: In the present study, we report a multidimensional analysis of behavioral and dispositional factors in real-time interactions between same and mixedneurotype dyads, identifying predictors of rapport and motivation for future encounters, and contrasting the diverse interaction characteristics of autistic and nonautistic adults.

Although the fact that autistic 1 people experience significant social interaction difficulties is widely agreed upon, it is debated if these difficulties are caused exclusively by the individual's deficits in social skills, as the traditional, clinical model suggests.
In this traditional model, autism is a disorder with persistent social deficits in communication and interaction across contexts (American Psychiatric Association, 2013).

As such, autistic people may have limited ability to 'read' other people's minds, interpret their behaviors, and they lack motivation to engage in social relations (e.g., Baron-Cohen et al., 1985; Chevallier et al., 2012).

text.text: However, more recent perspectives and greater involvement of the autistic voices in research have challenged these assumptions (e.g., Gernsbacher & Yergeau, 2019; Jaswal & Akhtar, 2018).

text.text: An alternative framework, the social model of autism aligned with the neurodiversity movement, views autism as a natural variation of human neurobiology.

In this model, social difficulty or disability experienced by autistic individuals comes at least partially from the inaccessible society built mainly in line with the needs and norms of the typically developing people who form the majority of the society.

Thus, the interactional difficulties emerge primarily from the mismatch between individuals of vastly different dispositions, like in the case of autistic and nonautistic neurotypes (Bolis et al., 2017; Milton, 2012).

text.text: At the same time, same-neurotype dyads -both autistic or both typically developing -often report having smoother and more successful interactions than mixed-neurotype pairs (Crompton, Hallett, et al., 2020; Crompton, Sharp, et al., 2020; McNaughton et al., 2024; Morrison et al., 2020; Rifai et al., 2022), which emphasizes the relative construction of the social meaning and the importance of compatibility with another person in relationships (Finke & Dunn, 2026).

text.text: Therefore, social challenges in autism may have both individual and relational origins.

In a recent review (Matyjek et al., 2025), we analyzed studies comparing autistic dyads with nonautistic or mixed-neurotype dyads (one of each neurotype), and found both behavioral similarities (e.g., general turn-taking) and differences (e.g., reduced mutual gaze and backchannelling -listener's signals like "yeah", "aha", or nodding) in autistic interactions.

text.text: The clearest differences between autistic and neurotypical interactions related to interpersonal (e.g., mutual gaze, backchannelling, reciprocal smiling), as opposed to intrapersonal (e.g., individual facial expressiveness, prosody, tendency to smile) behaviors.

Despite this relational nature of socially meaningful and observable behaviors, the strongest support for the social model of autism -with interactions being more successful in autistic than mixedneurotype pairs -came from studies measuring self-reported social interaction outcomes, like subjective ratings of rapport.
Because interlocutors cannot access each other's internal states directly, these subjective feelings of connection must be informed by the observable behaviors they witness in real time.
However, because past work has focused mainly on singular behaviors in isolation, it remains unclear which specific features-or combinations of features-drive these evaluations.

To determine what makes an interaction click, we need an approach that tracks multiple behaviors simultaneously, testing whether rapport is shaped by a partner's individual expressive style, the emergent coordination between them, or both.

Human social interaction is inherently complex, involving two or more agents who continuously generate and respond to information on multiple levels (Holler & Kuhlen, 2026; Holler & Levinson, 2019; Jaegher et al., 2010; see Figure 1A).

text.text: Each participant brings their own disposition to the interaction, including stable traits such as personality, social anxiety, tendency to mask or camouflage some behaviors, and reasoning skills, as well as transient states such as stress, fatigue, or momentary anxiety (Hessels et al., 2018; Neff et al., 2021).

text.text: Social interaction also depends on interactants' sociocognitive abilities, including theory of mind, emotion recognition, and empathy, and on their social motivation, that is, the willingness to engage and the reasons for doing so (Schilbach et al., 2013).

text.text: One level concerns intraindividual tendencies, such as a person's propensity to smile or to speak with a melodic prosody.

The other level concerns interpersonal coordination processes (driven by one or more interactants) that emerge between interactants, such as turn-taking, backchannelling, or behavioral synchrony (e.g., one person's smiling triggering the smile of the partner).

In real-time conversation, communicative cues systematically co-occur as composite multimodal signals that serve shared communicative functions (Enfield, 2009; Holler & Levinson, 2019; Trujillo & Holler, 2023).

text.text: Because different behavioral cues are often aligned functionally -despite differences in timescales (Hamilton et al., 2026) -they naturally cluster into coherent behavioral families (Van Kleef, 2017).

text.text: For example, one can nod and utter "oh, wow", both to provide listener feedback and contribute to interpersonal alignment.

Similarly, intraindividual expressivity and prosodic dynamics combine facial expressions, laughter, and pitch variation to signal personal warmth and communicative intents (Ambady & Rosenthal, 1992; Scherer, 2003).

text.text: Further, interpersonal dynamics unfold across distinct coordination systems: the discrete, structural rhythm of turn-taking that regulates conversational exchange (Levinson, 2016; Sacks et al., 1974), and the continuous non-verbal synchrony that binds interactants' movements and expressions into a shared temporal alignment (Tickle-Degnen & Rosenthal, 1990; Wheatley et al., 2012).

text.text: All these individual and dyadic processes jointly shape the outcomes of social interaction, which may include subjective evaluations of rapport, liking, and willingness to interact again, as well as more objective outcomes, including information transfer or joint task performance (Tickle-Degnen & Rosenthal, 1990; Vacharkulksemsuk & Fredrickson, 2012).

text.text: Defining successful interaction is not straightforward.
Sometimes, the goal of an interaction is to transmit information (e.g., giving someone directions to a train station).
Oftentimes, a goal (primary or secondarily) is to build connection.

In such settings, social success -and difficulty -have a subjective nature and different neurotypes may rely on different social behaviors in building their subjective judgements of interaction quality.
In neurodiverse interactions it is important not to assume that norms of typically developing individuals are the ground truth for interaction quality judgements.
For example, in neurotypical interactions, greater mutual gaze is often associated with more positive outcomes, such as increased satisfaction or liking (Senju & Johnson, 2009).
text.formatted: For example, in neurotypical interactions, greater mutual gaze is often associated with more positive outcomes, such as increased satisfaction or liking <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Senju & Johnson, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Yet this pattern does not necessarily generalize to autistic-autistic interactions (Crompton, Sharp, et al., 2020; Heasman & Gillespie, 2019).
text.formatted: Yet this pattern does not necessarily generalize to autistic-autistic interactions <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Crompton, Sharp, et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Heasman & Gillespie, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Further, even though autistic people are rated more negatively (social warmth, awkwardness, attractiveness) by both typically developing and other autistic observers, some studies show that both groups prefer to share future interactions with people of the same neurotype as their own (Morrison et al., 2020).

text.text: Thus, autistic individuals may be more 'forgiving' of unsuccessful exchanges and open to repeating an interaction regardless of the immediate first impressions.
Alternatively, they may simply rely on different social cues in the formation of the interaction quality judgements.
Deviations from typical development norms should therefore not be interpreted automatically as evidence of poorer interaction.
Instead, the quality of an interaction should be assessed with reference to the subjective experiences of each participant (Crompton, Sharp, et al., 2020; Milton, 2012).

text.text: This raises our central question: what predicts rapport or motivation for continuing the relationship, and for whom?
One likely source is a person's own disposition, which shapes how we interpret and experience the interaction.

For example, higher social anxiety may bias attention towards threat, increase self-consciousness, and thus contribute to a more negative subjective experience of the interaction (Nordahl et al., 2017).
text.formatted: For example, higher social anxiety may bias attention towards threat, increase self-consciousness, and thus contribute to a more negative subjective experience of the interaction <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Nordahl et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: A second source is the partner's behavior, from which impressions of warmth, confidence, and sociability are formed, and which in turn can influence liking and rapport (Ambady & Rosenthal, 1992; Gratch et al., 2007).

text.text: A third source is the degree of interpersonal coordination that emerges between the two interactants.

Real-time interactions involve constant prediction of the other's movements, which can help to attribute their affective, cognitive, and motivational states and adjust our actions accordingly to ensure a smooth and fluid interaction (Koban et al., 2019; Sebanz & Knoblich, 2009).

text.text: In neurotypical interactions, greater non-verbal coordination is associated with more positive outcomes, including liking, rapport, and interaction satisfaction (Vacharkulksemsuk & Fredrickson, 2012).

text.text: We therefore argue that, in dyadic interaction, an individual's subjective social outcomes are likely shaped by their own disposition (traits and states), their partner's behavioral tendencies (intonation and non-verbal expressivity), and the interpersonal dynamics that emerge between them, including both verbal and non-verbal domains (turn-taking, backchannelling, non-verbal synchrony; Figure 1B).

text.text: To identify predictors of social interaction outcomes, it is therefore necessary to observe multiple interactions in their natural behavioral flow and relate these patterns to individual subjective evaluation of the interaction.
Only recently has this become feasible, owing to advances in recording technology, automated behavioral analysis, computational power, and statistical methods.

We examined dispositional and behavioral predictors of self-reported rapport and social motivation in naturalistic online conversations between autistic, non-autistic, and mixed-neurotype dyads.

Overall, the results suggest that subjective social connection is shaped by a combination of individual dispositions, relational dynamics, and the specific pairing of two people, rather than by a stable set of individual behaviors or by neurotype alone.
Non-autistic dyads reported higher rapport than mixed-neurotype ones, whereas autistic dyads did not differ reliably from other pairing compositions.
At the same time, self-reported motivation to meet again did not differ between the dyad types.

This result does not provide clear support for either a strictly clinical account, which would predict poorer outcomes in autistic dyads, or a strong social-mismatch account, which would predict superior outcomes in autistic compared with mixed dyads.

It also cannot be explained by non-autistic individuals being better guessers of their partners' diagnosis status and showing an explicit same-neurotype preference: a secondary analysis suggested that both groups were similarly better in guessing partners matching their own neurotype.

Instead, it is consistent with evidence for a social privilege of non-autistic individuals, whose interaction style is often more readily recognized and rewarded as socially successful, including in brief interactions and first impressions (Morrison et al., 2020; Sasson et al., 2017; Sheppard et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Instead, it is consistent with evidence for a social privilege of non-autistic individuals, whose interaction style is often more readily recognized and rewarded as socially successful, including in brief interactions and first impressions <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Morrison et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Sasson et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Sheppard et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Such social privilege may contribute to the higher rapport observed in non-autistic dyads without necessarily implying that autistic people are intrinsically less able to form social connection.
The predictor models of rapport and social motivation shed light on what drives these evaluations.
Non-verbal synchrony was the only behavioral family emerging from dozens of considered behaviors that consistently predicted rapport.

This non-verbal synchrony was a composite reflecting greater temporal coordination in smiling, laughter, facial expressivity, and head movement, and was associated with stronger perceived rapport across dyad types and neurotypes.

This expands on a large body of work linking interpersonal coordination to affiliation, liking, interaction quality, and rapport (Fujiwara et al., 2026; Tickle-Degnen & Rosenthal, 1990; Tschacher et al., 2014; Vacharkulksemsuk & Fredrickson, 2012), a relationship shown to be causal through real-time manipulation of expressive alignment (Arias-Sarah et al., 2024).
text.formatted: This expands on a large body of work linking interpersonal coordination to affiliation, liking, interaction quality, and rapport <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Fujiwara et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Tickle-Degnen & Rosenthal, 1990;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Tschacher et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Vacharkulksemsuk & Fredrickson, 2012)</ref>, a relationship shown to be causal through real-time manipulation of expressive alignment (Arias-Sarah et al., 2024).

text.text: Our results extend this association to autistic and mixed-neurotype dyads and suggest that non-verbal synchrony may be a general relational process rather than a specifically nonautistic marker of successful interaction.

Recent work similarly indicates that autistic people can show social motor synchrony comparable to non-autistic people, even where subjective interaction experiences vary between dyad compositions (McNaughton et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Recent work similarly indicates that autistic people can show social motor synchrony comparable to non-autistic people, even where subjective interaction experiences vary between dyad compositions <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(McNaughton et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Remarkably, none of the intrapersonal behavioral families emerged as stable predictors of rapport or social motivation.
In other words, participants' rapport and social motivation ratings were not systematically predicted by how much one partner smiled, laughed, nodded, moved, spoke, or by their intonation tendencies.
This does not mean that these behaviors are irrelevant.
However, the dyadic, relational, interpersonal behaviors are more impactful on the emerging social outcomes.
For example, smiling frequently influences rapport when it elicits a reciprocal response from the partner.
Therefore, our findings support approaches that treat socially meaningful behavior as interactional rather than as a property of a single person (Jaegher et al., 2010; Sebanz & Knoblich, 2009).
text.formatted: Therefore, our findings support approaches that treat socially meaningful behavior as interactional rather than as a property of a single person <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Jaegher et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Sebanz & Knoblich, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: It is worth noting that beyond our specific behavioral findings, the overarching variance structure of the data provides statistical support for a relational account of social interaction.

By using a roundrobin design where each participant interacted with multiple partners, we applied Social Relations Modelling to decompose subjective outcomes into three sources: how a person generally evaluates others (rater effect), how a person is generally evaluated by others (partner effect), and the unique chemistry of a specific pairing (dyad effect).
For rapport, this unique dyadic effect accounted for the largest share of explained variance (43%), outweighing rater (32%) and partner effects (26%).
A similar relational contribution shaped social motivation to meet again, with dyad-specific effects accounting for 34% of the explained variance.

This relational complexity also explains why we found a large effect for non-autistic dyads reporting higher rapport than mixed-neurotype dyads even though the dyad type had limited rapport-predictive value (based on approximated Bayes Factors).

Similarly, our selected dispositional and behavioral features captured only a portion of the structured variance (fixed effects marginal R² values of .15-.20) compared to the total variance explained when accounting for the specific pairing of two individuals (total model conditional R² values of .68-.74).

Rapport and social motivation therefore reflect not only who people are, but also the particular combination of two people and numerous unmeasured features of the encounter, such as prior expectations, conversational content, shared interests, and momentary states (Ambady & Rosenthal, 1992; Hessels et al., 2018; Monnier et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Rapport and social motivation therefore reflect not only who people are, but also the particular combination of two people and numerous unmeasured features of the encounter, such as prior expectations, conversational content, shared interests, and momentary states <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Ambady & Rosenthal, 1992;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Hessels et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Monnier et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: A key strength of our exploratory, data-driven approach is precisely that it isolates stable predictive features-such as non-verbal synchrony-without flattening this complexity based on a priori decisions.
Social interaction outcomes were also predicted by the rater's dispositions.
Both rapport and social motivation were positively associated with cognitive engagement and negatively with autism-like traits.
Importantly, these associations did not vary by rater neurotype or dyad composition.

While the negative link with autism-related traits reflects the immediate burden of social anxiety and effortful selfmonitoring (Hull et al., 2017; Nordahl et al., 2017), the positive role of cognitive engagement highlights the executive demands of conversation.

text.text: This component integrated both stable traits (higher loading of reasoning and conscientiousness) and transient states (lower momentary stress and tiredness).

Real-time conversation is a fast-paced, predictive process: tracking cues, inferring intentions, and adapting responses in the moment requires attentional and executive bandwidth (Schilbach et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Real-time conversation is a fast-paced, predictive process: tracking cues, inferring intentions, and adapting responses in the moment requires attentional and executive bandwidth <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Schilbach et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Crucially, because this component spans both traits and states, it demonstrates that successful interaction depends not only on baseline cognitive resources, but on immediate access to them in the moment (Wilson & Hutcherson, 2026).
text.formatted: Crucially, because this component spans both traits and states, it demonstrates that successful interaction depends not only on baseline cognitive resources, but on immediate access to them in the moment <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">(Wilson & Hutcherson, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Given that navigating social environments can be disproportionately fatiguing and taxing for autistic adults (Hull et al., 2017), future research should move beyond static trait measures to track time-point-to-time-point fluctuations in stress and exhaustion, examining how the real-time depletion of cognitive resources shapes social outcomes over the course of an encounter.

text.text: Attitudes towards autism also predicted greater social motivation in autistic and mixed dyads, but not in non-autistic dyads.
Similarly, when looking at the neurotypes of each interactant instead of the dyadic composition, attitudes towards autism mattered when interacting with autistic, but not nonautistic partners.
This context-specific association suggests that positive beliefs about autism matter when autism is socially relevant to the interaction.
For example, attitudes may shape whether differences in conversational rhythm, expressivity, or other interactional features are interpreted as signs of incompatibility or as acceptable variation.

This aligns with evidence that autistic and non-autistic people can differ in how they interpret one another's behavior and mental states, and that social difficulty often reflects reciprocal misunderstanding rather than an individual autistic deficit (Crompton, Sharp, et al., 2020; Heasman & Gillespie, 2019).
text.formatted: This aligns with evidence that autistic and non-autistic people can differ in how they interpret one another's behavior and mental states, and that social difficulty often reflects reciprocal misunderstanding rather than an individual autistic deficit <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Crompton, Sharp, et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Heasman & Gillespie, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Positive attitudes may thus be one route through which people become more accommodating of individual atypical interactional styles.

Interestingly, in the model with both interactants' neurotypes, autistic participants reported higher social motivation overall than non-autistic participants, regardless of their partner's neurotype.
This finding challenges accounts that treat autism as involving a general reduction in desire for social contact (Chevallier et al., 2012).
text.formatted: This finding challenges accounts that treat autism as involving a general reduction in desire for social contact <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Chevallier et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Instead, it suggests that autistic people are motivated to pursue new social relationships even when interactions are effortful or when they experience greater stress or tiredness.

This pattern is consistent with accounts suggesting that reduced social participation in autism may reflect inaccessible social environments, repeated negative social experiences, anxiety, or limited opportunities rather than reduced interest of the individual (Jaswal & Akhtar, 2018; Milton, 2012).
text.formatted: This pattern is consistent with accounts suggesting that reduced social participation in autism may reflect inaccessible social environments, repeated negative social experiences, anxiety, or limited opportunities rather than reduced interest of the individual <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Jaswal & Akhtar, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Milton, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Autistic adults often report loneliness and barriers to developing satisfying relationships, yet loneliness is associated with factors such as social anxiety, limited social support, and dissatisfaction with available relationships rather than autism alone (Mazurek, 2014).
text.formatted: Autistic adults often report loneliness and barriers to developing satisfying relationships, yet loneliness is associated with factors such as social anxiety, limited social support, and dissatisfaction with available relationships rather than autism alone <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Mazurek, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Future studies should examine whether higher willingness to socially re-engage reflects greater openness to new connection, fewer opportunities for social contact, greater tolerance of interactional awkwardness, or some combination of these explanations.
In the light of this broader pattern of results, the association between autism-related traits and lower rapport tells a nuanced story.

On the one hand, this finding validates the lived experience of autistic people, for whom navigating social interaction is often cognitively and emotionally demanding, exhausting, and accompanied by the frustration of feeling misunderstood (Hull et al., 2017).
text.formatted: On the one hand, this finding validates the lived experience of autistic people, for whom navigating social interaction is often cognitively and emotionally demanding, exhausting, and accompanied by the frustration of feeling misunderstood <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Hull et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: On the other hand, because autism-like traits influenced rapport across all dyad types, this association should not be mistaken for a lack of social drive or inherent inability to connect in all autistic people.

Crucially, social difficulty does not equal a lack of social motivation: autistic participants in our study reported higher social motivation to meet again with their interaction partner, regardless of their neurotype, compared to non-autistic raters.

Furthermore, the "autism-related traits" component combined high loadings of autistic traits, social anxiety and camouflaging with low extraversion, and therefore likely captured a broader profile of social atypicalities rather than autism alone.

For example, social anxiety can increase concern about negative evaluation and self-focused attention, and camouflaging can make social participation cognitively and emotionally demanding (Cage & Troxell-Whitman, 2019; Hull et al., 2017; Nordahl et al., 2017).
text.formatted: For example, social anxiety can increase concern about negative evaluation and self-focused attention, and camouflaging can make social participation cognitively and emotionally demanding <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Cage & Troxell-Whitman, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Hull et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Nordahl et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, autism-related traits -and other primary drivers of the outcomes: non-verbal synchrony, cognitive engagement -cut across diagnostic borders, with similar effects in autistic, non-autistic, and mixed-neurotype interactions.

These findings show that clinical and social perspectives need not be mutually exclusive: while clinical frameworks capture the individual dispositions that make social navigation more effortful, the social model highlights how connection ultimately emerges through shared relational dynamics and mutual accommodation.
Several limitations should be considered.
First, interactions in this study took place online, where visual information, mutual gaze, bodily coordination, conversational timing, and social presence differ from in-person encounters.

Nevertheless, large-scale datasets of video-mediated conversations demonstrate that online interactions capture rich, ecologically valid interpersonal dynamics (e.g., the CANDOR corpus; Reece et al., 2023), and our replication of a synchrony-rapport association previously observed in face-to-face settings further suggests that online interaction reflects fundamental relational processes.
text.formatted: Nevertheless, large-scale datasets of video-mediated conversations demonstrate that online interactions capture rich, ecologically valid interpersonal dynamics (e.g., the CANDOR corpus; <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Reece et al., 2023)</ref>, and our replication of a synchrony-rapport association previously observed in face-to-face settings further suggests that online interaction reflects fundamental relational processes.

text.text: Second, this study did not examine conversational content or mutual gaze.

Topic selection, common ground, self-disclosure, humor, agreement, and repair of misunderstanding along dynamic negotiation of mutual gaze are likely to contribute substantially to rapport and to motivation for continued interaction.

Future research should integrate automated behavioral analysis guided by our feature selection results with linguistic, semantic, and discourse-level measures, and extend it to eye contact information.
Another valuable missing information would be quantification of participants' loneliness or social network.
This could shed light on whether the increased social motivation in the autistic group here was motivated by reduced current social opportunities.
Further, our sample size and demographic scope were modest.
Future work should test larger cohorts across wider age ranges and varied socio-demographic backgrounds.
Finally, the present study was exploratory and feasibility constrained.
Its value lies in taking a broad, data-driven view of interaction rather than testing one presumed marker of autistic social difficulty.
The selected effects should therefore be treated as targets for preregistered replication in larger and more diverse samples, rather than as exhaustive explanations of social connection.

Although our secondary models suggested that gender (mis)match, age difference, and language (English, Spanish) did not influence the pattern of reported results, future studies should examine whether these results generalize across diverse cultures, languages, genders, ages, communication modalities, and in-person settings, as well as across relationships that develop beyond a first encounter.
To conclude, our findings suggest that social interaction is not an individual performance against a fixed set of normative social skills.
On the contrary, social connection is created between people more than located within an individual.

While individual cognitive engagement supports the resources needed to interact, interpersonal non-verbal synchrony acts as the primary behavioral drive of rapport across diverse dyad compositions, showing how personal dispositions and relational dynamics jointly shape connection.
Autism makes this diversity especially visible because autistic people often navigate social environments built around non-autistic expectations.
Thus, autism provides a useful lens for studying variation in social dispositions in general, but diagnostic categories alone cannot explain how people experience an interaction.
Ultimately, all social interactions depend on fit, mutual interpretation, and shared adaptation.

Supporting connection should involve reducing the pressure to conform to a single normative interactional style and sharing the responsibility for mutual understanding across all interaction partners.

text.text: Sample size was determined in advance by time and funding constrains.
The maximum sample size was estimated at 60 participants balanced between autistic and non-autistic individuals.

Volunteers were recruited through participant databases of the Institute of Cognitive Neuroscience at the University College London (UK) and the Center for Brain and Cognition at the Universitat Pompeu Fabra (Barcelona, Spain).

Autistic participants were additionally recruited via X (Twitter), Prolific, UK-based autistic charity organizations (Autistica, Center for ADHD and Autism Support), internal communication within AIMS-2-TRIALS, informal peer networks within the autistic community, and the University of Sheffield's autistic contact list.
Non-autistic participants were additionally recruited via study flyers at University College London campuses.
The study protocol was approved by the Life and Medical Sciences Research Ethics Committee at UCL (approval number 59875/008).

All participants provided electronic informed consent forms and received financial compensation for their participation: €10 per hour for Spain-based participants or £10 per hour for UK-based participants.
Recruited volunteers were autistic or non-autistic adults between 20 and 35 years of age, fluent in English or Spanish, and with no self-reported learning disability nor speech impairment.
Autistic participants were required to confirm having a clinical autism diagnosis (e.g., Autism Spectrum Disorder, Asperger's Syndrome).

Non-autistic participants were excluded if they were under the care of a psychologist or psychiatrist (i.e., an NHS professional for UK-based participants or a clinical psychologist/psychiatrist for Spain-based participants).
From the initial cohort of 115 volunteers, 60 eligible individuals were invited to the experimental sessions.
All but one dyad met for the first time during the study.

Three participants (one English-speaking and two Spanish-speaking participants; one autistic and two non-autistic) did not show up and 1 participant was later rejected due to low quality of the collected video data, resulting in the final sample of N=56, 28 per group.

Each session comprised six participants (three individuals of each group).
Participants were never informed of others' neurotypes, and they never explicitly revealed their status in the study.
Each participant completed four dyadic interactions: two same-neurotype and two mixed-neurotype, yielding a total of 12 interactions per session.

Where a participant was missing (no-show, N=3), an experimenter completed the interaction with the unpaired participant to preserve the session structure; these interactions were excluded from analysis.

text.text: Participants first completed an online preexperimental survey with demographics and trait questionnaires (see Table 1).

text.text: Several days later, they attended a recorded Zoom session, accompanied by two experimenters.
Participants were assigned in pairs to three simultaneous breakout rooms across four interaction rounds.
Their self-view was disabled.
An experimenter was present in each breakout room with their camera and microphone disabled, monitoring passively.
Each interaction lasted 10 minutes and comprised two five-minute tasks.
First, dyads engaged in an unstructured 'get-to-know-you' conversation.
Optional prompts were provided to facilitate discussion (weather, pets, hobbies, etc.), but participants could select their own topics.
Second, dyads completed a word-description task inspired in the Taboo board game 2 .
In this article, we analyze only data from the unstructured conversation (however, the behavioral measurements correlated between the tasks, see section 2.2.6. in the Supplement).

After each interaction, participants completed a brief questionnaire rating their current states (stress, tiredness, anxiety) and evaluating the most recent interaction with another participants in terms of rapport and social motivation (more ratings were assessed in the study which are beyond the scope of this paper).
Both rapport and social motivation were rated on a 0-100 scale.
Participants were then allocated a new partner for the subsequent round.
Following the videoconference session, participants completed a post-experimental questionnaire with autism-related items (see Table 1).

text.text: Video was processed at 25 Hz with OpenFace v.

text.text: Dyadic synchrony for smiling, laughter, expressivity and head movement was indexed by the absolute mean cross-correlation across consecutive 30-s windows, evaluated over lags of 2s.
For each synchrony measure, observed dyads were compared against 1,000 shuffled pseudo-dyads to confirm that the observed synchrony was consistently greater in real than pseudo-dyads.

text.text: First, we tested whether rapport/social motivation varied with dyad type (AUT/NAUT/MIX).
Where appropriate, pairwise comparisons were corrected with Holm method.
Social Relations Models (SRM) were additionally calculated to explore the effects of the rater, partner, and dyad pairing.
Then, own dispositions, partner's behaviors and dyadic behavioral synchrony was analyzed to identify predictors of rapport/social motivation.

For all analyses, one's own self-reported rapport and social motivation were predicted with the parter's intraindividual behaviors (e.g., partner's tendency to smile, partner's backchannel count normalized by own total turn length), dyadic behavioral metrics (e.g., number of floor transitions), and one's own dispositional traits (e.g., autism-related traits).
This was done in three steps: dimensionality reduction, predictor selection, and mixed model testing.
We describe these steps below (see section 3 in the Supplement for more details).
First, dimensionality of the data with multiple predictors was reduced separately for dispositional and behavioral variables to handle multicollinearity issues (see Figure 1C and Figure 1D).

text.text: For disposition metrics, self-reported trait variables were reduced using Principal Component Analysis (PCA).

The strongest three components were retained and interpreted as: autism-related traits (high loadings of autistic, social anxiety, and camouflaging traits, low extraversion), attitudes towards autism (high loadings of attitudes, stigma, and familiarity with autism, low openness), and cognitive engagement (high loadings of reasoning skills and conscientiousness, low stress and tiredness).
See Figure 1D for the loadings of each disposition score on the three components.

See Figure 1C for a correlation plot between all behaviors and grouping into families.

In the second step, predictor selection, because of the large number of potential predictors and interaction terms, we used Ridge regression as a feature screening procedure to identify stable predictors of rapport and social motivation before fitting final inferential models.
We fit Ridge regression models using cv.glmnet function from glment v.
5.0 (Friedman et al., 2010) with a Gaussian outcome and alpha = 0 .
text.formatted: 5.0 <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Friedman et al., 2010)</ref> with a Gaussian outcome and alpha = 0 .

text.text: The initial design matrix included all main predictors and their interactions with the participant's neurotype (autistic/non-autistic).
Predictors were standardized, and model tuning was based on 10-fold cross-validation.
To avoid data leakage, folds were assigned at the participant level so that all observations from a given subject were kept within the same fold.
To evaluate coefficient stability, we performed a grouped nonparametric bootstrap with 500 resamples at the subject level.
In each bootstrap iteration, participant IDs were sampled with replacement.

To preserve the clustered structure of the data, duplicated bootstrap copies of the same participant were assigned unique bootstrap-specific IDs, and 10-fold cross-validation within each bootstrap sample was defined at this new ID level.
A Ridge model was refitted within each bootstrap sample, and coefficients at lambda.min (the penalty yielding minimum cross-validated prediction error) were stored.
Bootstrap inference focused on coefficient stability and effect size.

Features were selected for the final analysis if they met two criteria across the 500 resamples: (1) a mean absolute coefficient magnitude of at least 1.5, and (2) a sign stability of at least 80% (i.e., the coefficient was positive or negative in at least 80% of resamples).
To preserve structural hierarchy, main effects were automatically retained if their higher-order interaction terms were selected.
See Figure 4 for the results of the stability selection procedure.
text.formatted: See Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">4</ref> for the results of the stability selection procedure.

text.text: Given the large number of potential predictors and interaction terms in our dataset, multicollinearity was a clear issue.
Creating disposition components and behavioral families reduced this complexity, but testing all in mixed models still risked overfitting.
To address this, we used bootstrap Ridge screening to select only the predictors with stable effects before testing the predictors of rapport and social motivation.
The plot shows distribution of all candidate dispositional and behavioral predictors across 500 bootstrap resamples for rapport (left) and social motivation (right).

Each point represents a feature (a behavioral family, disposition component, or their interactions with rater's neurotype), plotted by its mean absolute penalized coefficient magnitude (i.e., mean absolute coefficient across the bootstraps; x-axis) and its sign stability (proportion of bootstrap iterations with the dominant coefficient direction; y-axis).
Plus and minus signs on the data points mark positive/negative dominant direction of the sign.

The top-right quadrant (white background) highlights the predefined selection space: features were retained for linear mixed-effects models if they fell into this quadrant, i.e., they met both an effect magnitude threshold of min.
1.5 (vertical dashed line) and a sign consistency threshold of min. 80% across resamples (horizontal dashed line).

In the final third step, mixed model testing, we fitted linear mixed-effects models (LMMs) to evaluate the impact of the selected predictors separately on rapport and social motivation using the lmerTest package v.
3.2.1. (Kuznetsova et al., 2017).
text.formatted: 3.2.1. <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Kuznetsova et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Fixed effects included the selected in step two behavioral and disposition predictors, alongside their interactions with (1) dyad type to explore dyad composition general effects, and (2) partner's and rater's own neurotype, to explore further autistic and non-autistic differences within the MIX dyads.
To account for the non-independence of dyadic data, models included crossed random intercepts for the actor, the partner, and the specific dyad.

Model parameters were estimated using the bobyqa optimizer, statistical assumptions were checked before interpretation with diagnostic plots, treatment contrasts were used, and main effects (across the threelevel dyad composition) were interpreted with ANOVA on the model.
Bayes factors (BF) were approximated using the Schwarz criterion (BIC; (Wagenmakers, 2007)).
text.formatted: Bayes factors (BF) were approximated using the Schwarz criterion (BIC; <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(Wagenmakers, 2007)</ref>).

text.text: Finally, three control variables: absolute age difference between the partners in a dyad, gender matching (binary:1 = match,0 = nonmatching), and language (English/Spanish) were added as fixed effects to test for their potential confounding effects.

Likelihood ratio tests and information criteria (AIC/BIC) indicated that these demographic controls did not improve model fit, so they were excluded from the final models, but are reported in section 4 of the Supplement.

Figure2Study design: round-robin.
Panel A) Each participant took part in one of 10 online sessions (5 in English and 5 in Spanish), in which they interacted with two persons of their neurotype and two of the other neurotype.
Panel B) This resulted in three dyad types: same-neurotype (both autistic or both non-autistic) and mix-neurotype.
Participants were not informed about the neurotype of their interaction partners.

Panel C) Eligible participants first completed a battery of standardized questionnaires and custom questions at home (see section 1 in Supplement for details), then joined the online session with five other participants, where over four rounds they interacted with their partners in dyads in three simultaneous digital break-out rooms.
After the online session, subjects completed final questionnaires (see section 1 in Supplement for details) and were debriefed and thanked for their participation.
